New Mexico State University Women’s Basketball

Session RPE Report, Part 2 – CMRJ x Load Correlations & Prediction · 2026-2027 Season

Dr. Luis Rodriguez Castellano

Data is current as of October 18, 2026

Report Overview

This report is a direct continuation of the Session RPE Report for the 2026-2027 season. Section 6 of that report introduced correlations between weekly training load and two VALD CMRJ outputs (takeoff jump height and rebound DRI) at the athlete-week and team-week resolutions. This Part 2 extends that work in three ways:

  1. A reliability pre-filter on all available CMRJ metrics (both first-jump and rebound), keeping only those with within-athlete CV% at or below 10%.
  2. A broader correlation panel across every reliable CMRJ metric against weekly sRPE, RPE Legs, RPE Lungs, and ACWR (EWMA ratio).
  3. A predictive step – can the variables we already track in daily_load meaningfully predict a jump metric of interest?

The practical intent: since sRPE is the primary routine load-tracking instrument, understanding how CMRJ outputs respond to that signal gives the coaching staff a second layer of context – which session types and intensity patterns the neuromuscular system responds to, versus which appear to pass through without a measurable jump response.

Why DRI instead of RSI? For the rebound portion of the CMRJ, the Dynamic Rebound Index (DRI) is preferred here over the standard RSI because it captures the elastic and reactive quality more completely than contact-time-normalized flight time alone, and tends to be the more stable discriminator across repeated tests in this cohort.

Coverage

  • Athletes included (post-cleanup): 15
  • Load-session rows retained: 859
  • CMRJ test sessions available: 184 across 28 distinct CMRJ metrics
  • Date range: Jun 16, 2026 – Oct 16, 2026

1. CMRJ Metric Reliability Pre-Filter

Before any metric is placed into a correlation matrix or a predictive model, each candidate CMRJ metric is screened for within-athlete reliability. A metric that bounces around between repeat tests of the same athlete can’t reflect training-induced change; any correlation it appears to have with load is driven by noise.

Threshold used: mean within-athlete CV% at or below 10% (adjustable in the YAML params block). The CV% is computed per athlete across her own repeat tests, then averaged across athletes to produce the metric-level figure in the table below.

2. Weekly Aggregation

Both the training-load variables (sRPE, RPE Legs, RPE Lungs, ACWR) and the reliability-filtered CMRJ metrics are collapsed to weekly athlete means for the correlation analysis. The joined dataset has one row per (athlete x ISO-week).

  • Athlete-week observations: 116
  • Team-week observations: 14

Both numbers matter for how to read the correlations below. Fewer observations means wider confidence intervals and more sensitivity to outliers. The athlete-week view has more data but mixes between- and within-athlete signal; the team-week view is cleaner but has fewer rows.

5. Predicting Jump Outcomes from Daily Load

This section asks the complementary question: can the weekly load variables actually predict a reliable CMRJ metric, rather than just correlate with it? For each reliable CMRJ metric, a linear mixed-effects model is fit at the athlete-week level with sRPE, RPE Legs, RPE Lungs, and ACWR as both a linear and a quadratic term so the model can capture the inverted-U load-response pattern (both low and high ACWR tend to suppress reactive output; the sweet spot is in the middle). Athlete is a random intercept so that each player has her own baseline jump value and the fixed-effect coefficients reflect within-athlete load-response rather than between-athlete differences.

5.1 Model specification

For each reliable CMRJ metric Y, the model is:

Y ~ s_rpe + rpe_legs + rpe_lungs + acwr + I(acwr^2) + (1 | athlete_id)

Fit with lme4::lmer; coefficients reported with 95% confidence intervals. The signature of the inverted-U load-response is a negative coefficient on I(acwr^2) combined with a positive coefficient on acwr – that’s the shape where output rises with moderate load and then falls off at the top end. If both ACWR terms are near zero the response is effectively flat; if the quadratic is near zero but the linear is non-zero, the response is linear for this cohort over this date range.

How to use these tables. The coefficient tells you how much the CMRJ metric is expected to change for a one-unit increase in that load variable, with every other load variable held constant and each athlete’s baseline absorbed by the random intercept. The 95% CI is usually more informative than the significance star – a tight CI around zero means “no effect of practical size,” while a wide CI even when non-significant means “we can’t tell yet, need more weeks.” Marginal R² indicates how much of the week-to-week jump variance the load variables alone can explain; conditional R² adds the share that simply reflects which athlete she is.

6. Interpretation for Coaching Staff

Three practical lenses for reading all of the above:

  • Load-to-performance direction. A negative correlation (or negative beta) between a reliable jump metric and s_rpe or rpe_legs suggests a load-induced depression of that quality: heavier weeks are associated with lower jump output. The magnitude matters more than the significance star when sample sizes are small.
  • Signal confirmation. rpe_legs and s_rpe should move together with jump output in the same direction if the signal is coherent. When they disagree, suspect one of them is noise (or that the relationship is non-linear, which the linear tools here can’t catch).
  • ACWR behavior is quadratic. The models above fit both a linear and a quadratic ACWR term so the inverted-U pattern can show up directly. A negative coefficient on I(acwr^2) with a positive coefficient on acwr indicates the classical sweet-spot shape; near-zero quadratic + non-zero linear would mean the response is effectively linear over the ACWR range this cohort has experienced so far this season. If neither term is distinguishable from zero and the CIs are wide, the honest reading is “we don’t have enough weeks yet to tell.”
  • Sign-flipped metrics are already oriented so higher = better. takeoff_countermovement_depth_cm and takeoff_ecc_peak_velocity_m_s are natively negative numbers (deeper CM / faster downward eccentric motion = more negative). They are inverted at ingest, so every column in the correlation and prediction tables reads the same way: positive r / positive β = better jump output.

What this does NOT tell you

  • Causality. Only randomized dosing of load against measured jump response can establish that.
  • Short-latency effects. Weekly aggregation hides anything that recovers within 24 hours.
  • Position / role differences. Guards and posts may respond differently to the same ACWR; this report pools positions. A split by position would need another iteration.
  • Multicollinearity. Jump height, flight time, peak concentric velocity, and others co-move mathematically; the correlation matrix may show redundant patterns across them. For predictive use, pick one representative per construct rather than trying to interpret all simultaneously.

Summary of Findings

A quick-read synthesis of the three sections above, aimed at the coaching and strength staff. Numbers refresh automatically each time the report is re-knit.

Reliability pre-filter. Of the 28 CMRJ metrics available for the season so far, 15 cleared the within-athlete CV% ≤ 10% threshold and are carried through to the correlation and prediction sections: takeoff_concentric_impulse_ns, takeoff_flight_time_ms, takeoff_rel_concentric_peak_power_w_kg, takeoff_concentric_peak_power_w, takeoff_peak_force_n, takeoff_concentric_peak_force_n, takeoff_rel_peak_force_n_kg, takeoff_rel_concentric_peak_force_n_kg, takeoff_ecc_peak_force_n, takeoff_contraction_time_ms, takeoff_ecc_decel_impulse_ns, takeoff_ecc_peak_velocity_m_s, takeoff_jump_height_cm, takeoff_countermovement_depth_cm, rebound_jump_height_cm.

Strongest signals (athlete-week level). The single largest-magnitude correlation was r = -0.37 between takeoff_ecc_peak_velocity_m_s and rpe_legs. Among positive associations, the strongest was r = +0.17 between takeoff_concentric_impulse_ns and rpe_lungs (higher weekly load → better jump output on this metric). Among negative associations, the strongest was r = -0.37 between takeoff_ecc_peak_velocity_m_s and rpe_legs (higher weekly load → lower jump output on this metric, consistent with a load-induced depression).

Prediction (mixed-effects, athlete as random intercept, predictors: sRPE, RPE Legs, RPE Lungs, ACWR, ACWR²). The jump outcome best predicted by the daily-load panel was rebound_jump_height_cm, with marginal R² = 0.07 (variance explained by load alone) and conditional R² = 0.85 (adding between-athlete differences). At a marginal R² below 0.10, the load panel does not yet carry enough signal on its own to anticipate week-to-week changes in this metric with confidence.

Practical read for the staff.

  • If the strongest correlations and the best R² point to the same CMRJ metric, that’s the metric to use as the team’s primary neuromuscular monitoring variable this season — the daily load panel is tracking it coherently from two angles.
  • If the correlation matrix is strong but the mixed-effects R² is weak, between-athlete differences are doing most of the work; interpret load → jump relationships per athlete rather than as a team-wide rule.
  • If both are weak, sRPE and ACWR are not yet carrying enough signal to anticipate CMRJ changes for this cohort over this date range. Keep collecting; revisit after another training block.
  • ACWR curvature. Check the sign of I(acwr^2) in Section 5.2 — a negative quadratic coefficient paired with a positive linear coefficient is the inverted-U signature and justifies monitoring the group for both detraining and overshoot zones, not just overshoot.

Data Notes

  • Source: daily_load and test_results tables in aggie.sqlite, joined to athletes for role identification.
  • Season start: 2026-06-01.
  • Load exclusions: main_focus = OFF rest days, DNP variants in comments, zero-effort / zero-duration rows, and days where availability was OUT or AS TOLERATED.
  • CMRJ exclusions: standalone rebound RSI metrics (rebound_rsi, rebound_reactive_strength_index) are dropped in favor of DRI for the rebound portion. Metrics with mean within-athlete CV% > 10% are then dropped from correlation and prediction.
  • Sign convention: takeoff_countermovement_depth_cm, takeoff_ecc_peak_velocity_m_s are natively negative (deeper CM / faster downward eccentric motion = more negative). They are inverted at ingest so that higher = better uniformly across the panel, which keeps the correlation heatmap and the regression betas pointing in the same direction as every other metric.
  • Correlation method: Pearson r (to match Part 1 Section 6.3c/d).
  • Prediction method: linear mixed-effects model via lme4::lmer with athlete as a random intercept, fitting both a linear and a quadratic term on ACWR (acwr + I(acwr^2)) to allow the inverted-U load-response shape to appear directly in the fit. Variance explained via performance::r2().
  • Analytic software: R 4.6.1, packages: tidyverse, lubridate, gt, lme4, broom.mixed, performance, ggcorrplot.
  • Anonymized render: rmarkdown::render(..., params = list(anonymize = TRUE))
